Question: Why is it so hard to believe WW2 happened for those who didn't live through it, why is WW2 so movie like in many ways?
Old_Answer: I did not live through WW2, but it is certainly not hard to believe or movie-like for me. I was born in Budapest, nearly 20 years after the war ended. Yet I grew up in a city where, especially in the smaller side streets, the scars of war were still all too readily visible. Damaged facades, bullet holes were everywhere in those old, turn-of-the-century mostly brick-and-mortar apartment buildings. (Many still have the scars in poorer, less well-maintained parts of the city or in spots not readily visible from the outside, such as internal courtyards.) And some historical buildings were still very much in ruins, such as those on historic Castle Hill on the Buda side. Another thing that was not terribly uncommon as I was growing up was the discovery of unexploded ordnance. Radio newscasts telling us that a street, an intersection was temporarily evacuated while bomb disposal teams were on scene neutralizing the threat. Still happens, by the way, though it’s much more of a rarity nowadays. More than that, my Mom lived through the siege of the city as small girl. She has many memories that she shared with me: The air raids that sent the family to the bomb shelter at Christmas, the damaged, looted apartment to which they returned many weeks later, corpses of humans and also horses, the latter sometimes surrounded by people who were carving them up for the meat. My grandmother still lived in that same apartment when I was growing up. She had a container, a large, shiny, repurposed aluminum can that she used to store flour. The can bore English-language markings courtesy of the American Red Cross, part of a post-war aid package to help a starving population. While my Mom and her family were hiding in that shelter, my father, much older, struggled to help his Jewish first wife and child and Jewish business partner with forged documents, which kept them out of the ghetto and ultimately, quite possibly kept them off the trains heading for Auschwitz. He could have been caught, carrying forged, still blank passports for instance when he was once stopped by an Arrow Cross patrol in late 1944. He was lucky: they did not search him. And of course the country I grew up in was at the time still occupied by forces of the USSR, the country that liberated the eastern half of Europe from Nazism, only to install their own version of totalitarianism in its place. So no, although (thankfully) I did not live through WW2, it is definitely not movie-like for me. People I knew, people close to me, but also places, buildings, streets all carried, sometimes still carry, tangible memories of that war.

Question: Why are black holes called black holes if they are actually white or lighter than the space around them?
Old_Answer: They are neither white nor lighter than the space around them. In classical general relativity, a black hole is truly black: it absorbs all light that hits it, and emits absolutely nothing. You really cannot get more black than that. Even with Hawking radiation, the situation is similar. Sure, black holes radiate. But astrophysical black holes have Hawking temperatures that are just a tiny, tiny fraction of the temperature of the cosmic microwave background radiation. In other words, even in this case, the black hole is a lot more black than the cosmos: it absorbs many orders of magnitude more radiation than it emits. So that’s why they are called black. Question: How is the speed of gravity determined?
Old_Answer: First of all, while I recognize that this is a bit of semantics, there is no “speed of gravity” any more than there is a “speed of electromagnetism”. Gravity is an interaction, it does not have an inherent speed. However, influences in the gravitational field, far from sources, travel as transverse waves, and these indeed do have a speed. Theory tells us that this speed is the same as the speed of influences in the electromagnetic field, i.e., electromagnetic waves such as light. While few had real doubts that this prediction is valid, its first observational test came seven years ago with the LIGO event GW170817. This gravitational wave event turned out to be the collision and merger of a pair of neutron stars, an event that was also detectable in a multitude of electromagnetic frequencies. The electromagnetic and gravitational signals arrived at the same time, even though they event took place some 130 million light years from here. This tells us that indeed, gravitational and electromagnetic waves traveled at the same speed. As a matter of fact, this had a direct impact on theory. There are proposed alternative theories of gravitation in which there is not one but two (or more) metrical fields, one determining the speed of gravitational waves, the other, the speed of electromagnetic waves. Question: What is quantum? Which things fit the definition of quantum?
Old_Answer: There are things that are “quantized”, which is to say, exhibit behavior that comes in distinct chunks, and the branch of physics that deals with these things is called therefore “quantum physics”. But to the extent that it even touches on the concept of “quantum”, it’s a consequence, not a foundation. Not anymore. At first, quantum physics was mostly empirical. Yes, it was based on the idea that atoms emit or absorb energy in such discrete chunks, or quanta. This was observed. This led, for instance, to Planck’s famous radiation law, which marks the dawn of quantum physics. But over time, we became a tad more sophisticated. Less then thirty years after Planck initiated his revolution, the “new” quantum theory of Heisenberg and Schrödinger emerged. It was no longer about atoms emitting and absorbing quanta, but something far more fundamental: the mathematical representation of the state of a physical system. In classical physics, constituent parts of a physical system can be characterized by a) where they are, b) how they move. In other words, their positions and their speed (or momenta). These can be represented by numbers. A position is just a set of coordinates. A velocity is a vector that can be characterized by a set of coordinates. As I said, numbers. Then comes the “new” quantum mechanics, which represents positions and momenta by… well, something else. Matrices in Heisenberg’s case, function operators in Schrödinger’s, but the bottom line is the same: These things are not numbers. Specifically, they do not behave like numbers do under multiplication. Take the momenta p and positions q of a system. In classical physics, we can multiply these numbers together and get a result that does not depend on the order of multiplication: p q = q p , or p q − q p = 0. But this is not how positions and momenta behave in the new quantum physics. They obey instead the relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant and, well, i = √ − 1 . This leads to all sorts of weird consequences, which have been confirmed experimentally. Among other things… well, quanta. Take one of the simplest physical systems, a simple oscillator (the so-called harmonic oscillator). Describe it in terms of these non-commuting variables and you get a weird result: The oscillator cannot have arbitrary energies. Its energy is discretized, going up or down by one unit, or quantum at a time. Electrons in an atom are well described by such oscillators as a mathematical model. So there we have it, the quantized behavior of how atoms emit or absorb energy. But quantum physics in general is not really about quanta. It’s not about chopping things up into small units. That might have been the original inspiration more than a century ago, but it has become something much more nuanced. Planck’s quanta are still there, but as a consequence, not as a building block, of the theory. There are plenty of “quantum” systems that have no quantized behavior. E.g., a free particle can have any energy; nothing “quantized” there. The fundamental statement of the theory is not about quanta; it is about the behavior of those key variables, the positions and momenta of a physical system, and how this behavior is described by the mathematics of noncommuting things, as opposed to the mathematics of simple numbers. Like it or not, that is how Nature behaves, as demonstrated by countless experiments. That said, when we go beyond simple quantum mechanics into the realm of quantum field theory, things change a bit. A field, like the electromagnetic field, can be described as a sum of, well, pure waves really, by way of what is called a Fourier-transform. Each of these pure waves behaves like a harmonic oscillator, which we know how to describe using quantum physics. Each of these harmonic oscillators is characterized by those distinct chunks of energy by which the oscillator’s energy can increase or decrease. In quantum field theory, these distinct chunks of energy (and possibly other conserved properties, like charge or angular momentum) turn out to be none other than the things we’ve know, we’ve observed, as particles! So there you have it: elementary particles come closest to the concept of “quantum”.
